analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC sue drug companies that file baseless FDA petitions to delay generic competition.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee unanimously reported the bill to the floor in April 2025, and it now sits on the Senate calendar awaiting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes file petitions with the FDA raising supposed safety concerns about a generic competitor — petitions the FDA often finds baseless — because the FDA generally cannot finish approving the generic while a petition is pending, buying the brand-name company extra months of sales without competition. This bill makes filing such petitions to interfere with a competitor an unfair method of competition. The Federal Trade Commission could sue the filer and win civil penalties: the greater of $50,000 per day the FDA spent reviewing the sham petition, or the revenue the company earned from the drug while the petition was pending.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars: removing sham petitions speeds approval of lower-cost competitors, which tend to drive down prices. It also helps generic and biosimilar manufacturers, who currently lose months of market time to petitions the FDA itself has called dilatory.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying for prescriptions; generic drug makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it an unfair method of competition for a person to submit a 'sham' FDA petition — one that is objectively baseless and that attempts to use the petition process, rather than its outcome, to interfere with a competitor's approval — including a series of such petitions filed against the same application.

The FTC may bring a civil action against the filer, and the penalty is the greater of $50,000 for each calendar day the sham petition was under FDA review or the revenue the company earned on the drug during that period, making delay potentially far more expensive than it is profitable.

If the Secretary of Health and Human Services determines a petition in a series was filed primarily to delay approval and refers it to the FTC, the petition is presumed part of a sham series unless the defendant proves otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence.

The bill states it does not limit petitions filed in good faith to raise legitimate public health concerns, and leaves all existing antitrust and FTC remedies in place; it applies only to petitions filed on or after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers that file baseless petitions: they face FTC lawsuits and civil penalties sized to the delay's value, and lose a proven tool for stretching out periods without generic competition. There is no general taxpayer cost; the FTC would bear routine enforcement costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug manufacturers filing baseless petitions

drawbacks.text: The bill's penalty is potentially enormous because it can equal a company's entire revenue on a drug during the review period, which critics of such measures argue goes well beyond what is needed to deter sham filings and could produce outsized settlements.

The presumption triggered by an HHS referral is largely shielded from judicial review, and an honest objection is that the threat of large penalties could chill companies from filing petitions raising genuine safety questions about generics and biosimilars, even though the bill is written to protect good-faith petitions.
The FDA already has authority under the same statute to summarily deny petitions filed to delay, so the bill adds an antitrust enforcement layer rather than fixing the underlying review bottleneck.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: drug delay tactics that the FDA has repeatedly flagged get a real price attached, and patients reach cheaper generics sooner. The main cost is the risk of over-deterrence — a company facing revenue-sized penalties may stop filing even legitimate safety petitions. The bill tries to manage that by limiting it to objectively baseless filings and shielding good-faith petitions, but enforcement will show whether that line holds. On balance the design is targeted rather than sweeping.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it without amendment and it was placed on the Senate's general calendar in April 2025, where it awaits a floor vote that no one has scheduled.

narrative.text: Introduced March 24, 2025 by Senator Klobuchar with six original cosponsors, including Republicans Grassley and Cruz alongside Democrats Durbin, Blumenthal, Welch, and Booker.

On April 3, 2025 the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and on April 10 it was reported and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 45 — the list of bills eligible for floor consideration.
No floor vote has been scheduled since; the Congress is still in session, so the bill's fate remains open.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, brand-name drug makers are better off: the bill is stalled on the calendar without a scheduled vote, so the existing ability to file baseless petitions that delay generic approval remains intact and unpenalized.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: Lead sponsor; Senate Democrat from Minnesota
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop STALLING Act to give the FTC authority to penalize sham FDA petitions that delay generic drugs.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: Senate Judiciary Committee member; Republican from Iowa
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and, as reporting member, reported it out of committee without amendment on April 10, 2025.

for.name: Sens. Durbin, Blumenthal, Welch, Booker, and Cruz
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing from the start.

against.name: Senate floor leadership (unnamed in the record)
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a floor vote in the months since it was placed on the calendar.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Manufacturers of originator drugs that use the FDA citizen-petition process
against.what_they_did: Has publicly opposed bills targeting sham citizen petitions in past Congresses, arguing FDA already screens petitions and the measures are unnecessary; no formal opposition to this bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 2 Republican and 4 Democratic cosponsors, and it cleared the Judiciary Committee favorably without amendment; no opposition vote is recorded, and the only obstacle so far is the absence of a scheduled floor vote.

industries.note: The bill attaches civil penalties — up to a drug's full revenue during the review period — to baseless FDA petitions used to delay generic approval, removing a tactic that keeps cheaper competitors off the market for months. Patients pay the cost of those delays today.
Fewer sham petitions means faster FDA decisions on generic applications and earlier market entry, which is also when prices for patients fall.
The bill creates a new civil enforcement tool against sham petitions, adding to the FTC's competition authority.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is a repeat of similar measures that cleared the Judiciary Committee in earlier Congresses but never received a Senate floor vote. With bipartisan sponsorship and a favorable committee report in hand, a vote is possible if leadership makes time, but most bills sitting on the general calendar without leadership attention at this stage die when the Congress ends. A House companion moving in parallel would improve its odds.
